extracted.intended_audience: researchers and practitioners designing or studying blockchain-enabled AI systems (system designers, AI engineers, blockchain architects)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for selecting blockchain architectures, infrastructures, and consensus protocols suitable for AI applications, and for designing decentralized AI/data systems (e.g., for healthcare, IoT, robotics, supply chains).

rubrics_metrics.name: Private blockchain characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: A private blockchain is managed by a single organization. Unlike public blockchains, the private blockchains are designed as permissioned systems where users and participants in the systems are pre-approved for read/write operations and are always known within the network.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Private blockchains are comparatively faster due to known identities of validators and pre-approved participants; they require less complex mathematical operations to validate transactions. They can transfer any kind of indigenous data, values, and assets. Transaction approval/asset transfer approvals are managed using voting or multiparty consensus algorithms which consume low energy and enable fast transactions. Transaction approval time usually remains lower than one second.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consortium (federated) blockchain characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Consortium blockchains (a.k.a. federated blockchains) are operated by a group of organizations usually formed based on mutual interests of participating organizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Like private blockchains, consortium blockchains operate as permissioned systems, but only a few participants can perform write operations while usually all participants can read. They are comparatively faster than public blockchains due to pre-approved participants with known identities and consume less energy because of voting-based or multiparty approval consensus protocols. Typical transaction approval on federated blockchains gets approval within one second.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blockchain-as-a-Service (BaaS) suitability
rubrics_metrics.description: Cloud service providers offer environments to develop and test blockchain services (BaaS) for customers, enabling development without handling underlying infrastructure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: BaaS benefits private and consortium blockchain companies by allowing focus on application development, testing, and deployment. Developers gain single-click provisioning to write smart contracts. Integration of BaaS with existing AI cloud services opens opportunities for developers and cross-industry consortia.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linear (single-chain) infrastructure suitability
rubrics_metrics.description: Single chain-based blockchain architectures grow linearly where new blocks are appended at the chain. Early decentralized systems operate on single chains but these systems have multiple issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Single chains scale slowly and can compromise real-time performance; separate single chains are required for each business scenario, making multi-chain value/information exchange impossible. Single-chain blockchains can be used for single-task AI applications (search, optimization, learning) or to store only performance histories (e.g., model performance logs), but putting whole AI application components on chain is generally not feasible due to unconstrained environments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonlinear (multichain) infrastructure suitability
rubrics_metrics.description: Nonlinear blockchain architectures are implemented as multichain architectures (parent-child chains, main-side chains, parallel chains). One or more chains keep information about other chains and serve as main chains while others act as side/child/parallel chains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multichain architectures are scalable for real-time performance and support diverse business scenarios and cross-chain value transfers (e.g., two-way pegging). They facilitate execution of multiple interrelated or independent AI tasks, allow parallel development and deployment (training/testing on side chains or testnets, production on main chain), and benefit reinforcement/adaptive learning workflows that require continuous retraining.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decentralized infrastructure characteristics relevant to AI
rubrics_metrics.description: Blockchain infrastructure introduces decentralized and shared control, immutable audit trails, and native asset exchanges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combined with AI, these traits provide new data models, shared control of AI training data and models, and improved trustworthiness of data. They support secure data provenance, tamper-proof records, and mechanisms for monetizing/controlling personal data (e.g., decentralized healthcare data marketplaces).

rubrics_metrics.name: AI operational requirement: high write-frequency and latency sensitivity
rubrics_metrics.description: AI applications have high frequency of write operations because intelligent algorithms continuously update decision structures for informed decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consensus protocols and chain architectures that introduce high latency or long validation times (e.g., energy-intensive PoW with long mining times) become performance bottlenecks for real-time AI tasks, streaming data ingestion, and real-time informed decisions. Choose low-latency, energy-efficient consensus or permissioned architectures for real-time AI.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof of Work (PoW) - evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: PoW requires a large number of anonymous validating nodes to mine blocks by solving complex mathematical problems; new transactions are added when sufficient nodes solve the problem (e.g., 51%).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PoW is energy intensive and increases transaction approval delay; it can be a performance bottleneck for AI applications with frequent writes. Public PoW-based systems are also vulnerable to 51% attacks that can compromise security for AI applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof of Stake (PoS) - evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: PoS selects validators based on stake (e.g., coin holdings, delegation, transaction frequency).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PoS is more energy-efficient than PoW and mitigates anonymous validators, but validators may have little immediate penalty for not validating causing potential delays in block creation. PoS can be useful for delay-tolerant AI applications but is less suitable for streaming or real-time AI that need low-latency updates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Byzantine Fault Tolerance (BFT) - evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: BFT is a majority voting algorithm that rules out validations from malicious nodes already part of the blockchain network and handles fault tolerance when a sufficient fraction of nodes are non-faulty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although implementation is challenging, BFT variants (e.g., requiring two-thirds non-faulty nodes, digital signatures, constrained peer communication) have been used in critical systems and could be valuable for AI applications that require strong fault tolerance and security.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof of Activity (PoAc) - evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: PoAc is a hybrid of PoW and PoS: initially operates with PoW to bootstrap stake and then enables PoS for validators with acceptable stake.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PoAc can be efficient in security, storage, and network communication and may suit AI applications that require higher security and lower data availability demands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof of Burn (PoB) - evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: PoB allows validators to be eligible only if they 'burn' coins (send to a verifiable unspendable address); after burning, they may create new blocks and receive rewards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PoB reduces energy consumption relative to PoW, can balance coin supply and incentivize initial investment. The paper suggests PoB can be used to incentivize users to maintain values such as model accuracy or minimum numbers of discovered objects (e.g., by 'burning' learning models/search trees to maintain value).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof of Elapsed Time (PoET) - evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: PoET finds a leader by associating a random timer with each node and selecting the node with minimum expiry to create the block.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PoET is energy-efficient but random timer assignment can introduce waiting delays; it may slow AI systems that cannot tolerate waiting and is more suitable for delay-tolerant applications. It also allows detection of malicious users if the same nodes are repeatedly selected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof of Capacity (PoC) / Proof of Space - evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: PoC (proof of space) uses hard drive space as the resource where nodes store precomputed nonce values and nodes with large disk space have higher probability of unlocking blocks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PoC reduces computational mining intensity (relative to PoW) by leveraging storage, changing the resource trade-offs for validator selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof of Authority (PoA) - evaluation and governance requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: PoA delegates authoritative control to specific nodes which collectively form consensus based on majority votes; validators are known and legitimate stakeholders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PoA is energy efficient and introduces minimal delay and is well-suited for private or consortium networks. Implementers must consider legal identity of validators, well-defined eligibility criteria, and universal eligibility standards. Security risks remain high because compromised validators can attack the network.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof of Importance (PoI) - evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: PoI ranks and weights validators based on frequency of successful validations; validators with high frequency get more importance and their approvals over-weigh others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PoI can create high trust among participating nodes and be useful on public blockchains. In private or consortium settings it risks monopolization and stakeholder conflicts because important validators can dominate the network.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consensus-protocol choice as an application-fit criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Different consensus protocols impact performance, security, energy consumption, and suitability for AI workloads.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing blockchain-enabled AI applications, select consensus protocols by matching protocol trade-offs (energy, latency, validator identity, resistance to attacks, governance) to AI requirements (real-time streaming vs delay-tolerant, privacy, security, throughput). The paper lists many protocols (PoW, PoS, BFT variants, PoAc, PoB, PoET, PoC, PoA, PoI) and notes newer options (Proof of Luck, Proof of Exercise, etc.) for exploration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data/storage and compute requirements for AI on blockchain
rubrics_metrics.description: AI requires huge datasets and high computing power for training; blockchains and decentralized storage/compute can be combined to meet these needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use decentralized storage (e.g., IPFS) and decentralized compute frameworks (e.g., distributing parts of neural nets across nodes) to scale. Consider off-chain storage or side chains for heavy model artifacts and only store performance or provenance data on-chain. Designs like ChainIntel and PBFT-DPOC (delegated proof of contribution) are examples addressing compute/storage mapping and throughput/latency trade-offs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privacy-preserving/federated learning with blockchain
rubrics_metrics.description: Federated learning when unified with blockchain and cryptography can improve privacy by ensuring data are not centrally stored in the cloud while enabling decentralized model training.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blockchain can record provenance and aggregated model updates, while tokens/incentives can encourage users to share encrypted data or model contributions (e.g., Snips AIR uses blockchain and tokens to keep personal voice data local and aggregate training on-chain). This approach helps avoid sharing raw personal data, addressing privacy risks in cloud-hosted AI assistants.
